You cannot make it a **premise-free** proof that forces assent from everyone. Philosophy does not work that way. But you can make it a rigorous argument whose conclusion follows if its premises are granted.\n\nThe best steelman is the **Aristotelian–Thomistic contingency/act-potency argument**. Here it is in a clean form.\n\n---\n\n### Steelmanned argument for a prime mover\n\n**Key terms**\n\n- **Contingent being**: a being that can exist or not exist. Its essence is distinct from its existence.\n- **Necessary being**: a being that cannot not exist. Its essence entails its existence.\n- **Essentially ordered causal series**: a series of simultaneous ontological dependence, not a temporal chain. Each member depends on a prior member here and now for its causal power or existence.\n- **Potency / act**: potency is the capacity to be or become something; act is the actuality of being or doing.\n\n**Premises**\n\n1. Some contingent concrete things exist.  \n   *Empirical starting point: we exist, but we need not have existed.*\n\n2. Every contingent thing has a sufficient ontological ground for its existence—either in another contingent thing or in a necessary being.  \n   *Restricted Principle of Sufficient Reason. Nothing contingent explains itself.*\n\n3. There cannot be an infinite essentially ordered series of contingent grounds.  \n   *If every member borrows its existence from another, the whole series is still borrowed. An infinite series of borrowed existence does not explain why anything exists at all.*\n\n4. Therefore, there must be a necessary being.  \n   *From 1–3.*\n\n5. A necessary being cannot have any potency for non-existence or for any perfection it lacks.  \n   *If it could lack existence, it would be contingent. If it could gain or lose a perfection, it would be changeable.*\n\n6. Therefore, the necessary being is pure actuality (*actus purus*).  \n   *No potency in it at all.*\n\n7. Pure actuality is simple—no composition of essence and existence, form and matter, potency and act.  \n   *Composition implies dependence on parts, which would make it contingent.*\n\n8. A simple, pure actuality is immaterial, eternal, immutable, and the source of all being, order, and goodness.  \n   *Matter involves potency; change involves potency; limitation involves potency.*\n\n9. Therefore, there exists a prime mover: an unmoved, uncaused, self-existent, non-physical first cause of all dependent reality.\n\n---\n\n### What this proves\n\nIf you accept premises 1–3, the argument validly yields a **necessary ground of contingent reality**. Steps 5–8 then add classical metaphysical claims: that this ground is pure actuality, simple, immaterial, eternal, and the source of all being.\n\nThis is enough to establish a **prime mover** in the classical sense: not a first event in time, but the atemporal ontological ground of everything that exists dependently.\n\nTo get the **full classical theistic conclusion**—intellect, will, omnipotence, omniscience, omnibenevolence, creator—you need further arguments:\n\n- **Intellect and will**: The first cause is the source of all perfections. Intellect and will are perfections. Therefore they exist in it pre-eminently. Or: it moves as final cause, which requires intelligibility and goodness.\n- **Omnipotence**: Pure actuality has no limitation on its causal power.\n- **Omniscience**: Pure actuality is the source of all truth and intelligibility, so it knows all things.\n- **Omnibenevolence**: Being, truth, and goodness are convertible in classical metaphysics. Pure actuality is infinite being, hence infinite goodness.\n- **Creator**: The first cause grounds all being. Creation *ex nihilo* is a further theological specification, but ontological dependence is already established.\n\nThese steps are not automatic. They require additional classical metaphysical premises. But they are not arbitrary either—they are the standard Thomistic extensions.\n\n---\n\n### The honest verdict\n\n**Yes**, it is possible to construct a valid deductive proof of a prime mover.\n\n**No**, it is not possible to construct a proof that is *standalone* in the sense of requiring no controversial premises. The argument depends on:\n\n- a strong Principle of Sufficient Reason,\n- rejecting brute facts and infinite regresses,\n- treating physical reality as contingent,\n- accepting act/potency metaphysics,\n- and treating existence, truth, and goodness as convertible.\n\nIf someone denies those premises, they can consistently deny the conclusion. They may say: “The physical universe is just brute.” Or: “The physical universe is necessary.” Or: “An infinite regress is acceptable.” Those are logically possible. It either multiplies brute facts or stops being brute-fact theory.**\n\nIf you say, “Only one thing is brute, everything else needs a reason,” then ask: why is that the rule?\n\n- If the answer is **“It’s just brute,”** then you now have at least two brute facts:\n  1. The first cause exists.\n  2. The rule that only the first cause is brute.\n\nSo you no longer have “only one brute fact.” You have a brute fact plus a brute distribution rule.\n\n- If the answer is **“It follows from the nature of the first cause,”** then the first cause is not brute. Its nature explains why it alone is ultimate. That is exactly what classical self-existence means: its essence entails its existence, and everything else depends on it.\n\nSo the defender’s move either adds more brute facts, or it converts the first cause into a self-existent ground. It cannot keep both “only one brute fact” and “brute fact” without equivocation.\n\n**2. Symmetry, elegance, and parsimony are not logical laws.**\n\nReality does not have to be symmetric. There is no rule that if one thing is brute, all things must be brute. So the objection from symmetry is not a proof. But it is a clue. An ultimate explanation that says “one arbitrary stop, and then everything else is explained” is less intelligible than one that says “the ultimate is self-explanatory, and everything else depends on it.” The second is more parsimonious: one self-existent ground, no brute facts.\n\n**3. “The only objective truth” is doing too much work.**\n\nA brute fact is just an unexplained actuality. It does not thereby become the “only objective truth” that all subjective views must trace back to. That is an extra claim. If it is brute, then it is just posited. If it is necessary, then it is self-existent. Truths alone do not cause or ground existence. Mathematical truths are objective, but they do not make subjective views trace back to them. So this part of the defender’s reply is not an explanation; it is a poetic restatement of the problem.\n\n**4. The classical answer is not an arbitrary asymmetry.**\n\nThe classical theist says the asymmetry is not brute. It follows from the nature of ultimacy:\n\n- The ultimate cannot be composed, or it would depend on its parts.\n- It cannot be contingent, or it would need a ground.\n- It cannot be one of many, because distinction implies limitation, composition, or potency.\n- Therefore there can be exactly one simple, necessary, self-existent ground.\n\nThat is not a brute rule. It is a consequence of what it means to be ultimate. So the classical view satisfies parsimony better than the brute-fact defender’s move: one self-existent ground, no brute facts, no dangling asymmetry.\n\n**Conclusion:**\n\nThe defender can say, “That asymmetry is just another brute fact.” But then they have not saved the one-brute-fact view. They have either admitted multiple brute facts or turned the first cause into a self-existent ground. The move is logically possible, but it is ad hoc, unstable, and ultimately unintelligible. It leaves you dangling. I will state it in classical metaphysical terms, defend each move, and then give the most rigorous conclusion it can bear. I will use **ontological ground** rather than “topological cause,” because “topological” suggests spatial or mathematical topology. What is meant is an atemporal order of dependence: what explains what, not what happened before what.\n\n---\n\n## The Steelmanned Contingency Argument for a Prime Mover\n\n### Key definitions\n\n- **Contingent being**: a being that can exist or not exist. Its essence is distinct from its existence. It does not contain its own existence.\n- **Necessary being**: a being that cannot not exist. Its essence entails its existence.\n- **Self-existent (strong sense)**: a being whose nature is to exist. It is not merely uncaused; it is self-explanatory.\n- **Brute fact (weak sense)**: something that is uncaused but whose nature does not entail its existence. It just happens to exist.\n- **Essentially ordered series**: a series of simultaneous ontological dependence. Each member depends on another here and now for its existence or causal power. This is not a temporal chain.\n- **Pure actuality**: a being with no potency, no unrealised capacity, no composition, no limitation.\n\n---\n\n### The core deduction\n\n1. **Some contingent concrete reality exists.**  \n   We exist, and we need not have existed. The physical universe, as far as we know it, is contingent.\n\n2. **Every contingent concrete reality has a sufficient ontological ground.**  \n   This is a restricted Principle of Sufficient Reason. It does not say everything needs a cause. It says everything that is contingent needs a ground. A contingent thing cannot explain itself, because its essence does not entail its existence.\n\n3. **An essentially ordered series of contingent grounds cannot be infinite.**  \n   If every member borrows its existence from another, the whole series is still borrowed. Adding more borrowers does not create a lender. An infinite series of dependent things never explains why there is anything at all. This is not about time. Even an infinite past would still be a dependent whole.\n\n4. **Therefore, there must be a necessary ground of contingent reality.**  \n   From 1–3.\n\n5. **A necessary ground cannot have any potency, composition, or limitation.**  \n   If it could lack existence, it would be contingent. If it could gain or lose a perfection, it would be changeable. If it were composed of parts, it would depend on those parts. So it must be pure actuality, simple, immaterial, eternal, and immutable.\n\n6. **Therefore, there exists a unique, simple, immaterial, eternal, self-existent, necessary being—the prime mover—on which all contingent reality depends.**  \n   This is the core conclusion.\n\n---\n\n## Defending the Premises\n\n### 1. Why every contingent thing needs a ground\n\nA contingent thing’s existence is not contained in its essence. It is a fact that it exists, but not a fact that follows from what it is. So its existence must be grounded either in another contingent thing or in a necessary being. If only in another contingent thing, we have not yet explained it. We have only deferred the question.\n\n### 2. Why an infinite regress fails\n\nAn infinite regress of contingent things is logically possible. But it is not an explanation. It explains each member by another, but never explains the series as a whole. If every member is borrowing existence, the whole series is still a borrower. You cannot get a lender by adding more borrowers. So an infinite regress leaves ultimate reality unintelligible. It is a refusal to complete the explanation.\n\n### 3. Why brute fact fails\n\nA brute fact is uncaused, but it is not self-existent in the strong sense. Its nature does not entail its existence. It just happens to exist. If you say the universe is brute, you are saying it is uncaused but contingent. But contingent things need a ground. If you say it does not need a ground, you have denied the Principle of Sufficient Reason. If you say it is necessary, then it is not brute; it is self-existent. So brute fact cannot be the ultimate stopping point if you demand a complete explanation. It leaves you dangling.\n\n### 4. Why physicalism cannot be the ultimate ground\n\nPhysical reality is either contingent or necessary.\n\n- If contingent, it needs a ground beyond it.\n- If necessary, its essence must entail existence.\n\nBut physics describes mass, charge, spin, field, law, symmetry, structure, relation, and dynamics. It tells you how something behaves **if** it exists. It does not tell you why it exists. Physical nature does not entail existence. So physical reality cannot be the ultimate self-existent ground unless you add a further argument showing that physical nature is necessary. That argument is not available from physics alone.\n\n### 5. It gives necessity without existence. It cannot cause or instantiate a concrete universe. It cannot be the first cause. It may be grounded in the necessary being’s intellect, but by itself it is not the prime mover.\n\n### 6. It is the most parsimonious and intelligible stopping point.\n\n---\n\n## Extending to the Full Classical Theistic Conclusion\n\nThe core argument establishes a necessary, simple, immaterial, eternal, self-existent prime mover. To reach the full God of classical theism, you need further arguments:\n\n- **Intellect**: The first cause is the source of all order and intelligibility. To cause by finality requires knowledge. All perfections pre-exist in it. Intellect is a perfection. Therefore it is intellectual.\n- **Will**: It is not compelled by anything outside itself. It acts freely.\n- **Omnipotence**: Pure actuality has no limitation on its causal power.\n- **Omniscience**: It is the source of all truth and intelligibility, so it knows all things.\n- **Omnibenevolence**: Being, truth, and goodness are convertible in classical metaphysics. Infinite being is infinite goodness.\n- **Creator**: It grounds all being. Creation ex nihilo is a further theological specification, but ontological dependence is already established.\n\nThese steps require additional classical premises. But they are not arbitrary. Every contingent concrete being has a sufficient ontological ground.  \n   *This is the restricted Principle of Sufficient Reason. It is a substantive premise, not a definitional truth.*\n\n3. A complete ground cannot consist solely of derivative grounds whose grounding efficacy is itself entirely derived.  \n   *This is the anti-regress premise. It is not the same as “adding borrowers does not create a lender.” It says: a series composed entirely of borrowed grounding cannot be the complete ground of the series.*\n\n**Core conclusion:**\n\n> Therefore, at least one non-derivative ground of contingent concrete reality exists.\n\nThat is what the core argument can validly establish, if its premises are granted. It does **not** yet establish that this ground’s essence entails its existence. It does **not** yet establish simplicity, immateriality, eternity, or uniqueness.\n\n---\n\n## What is needed for the classical prime mover\n\nTo move from “non-derivative ground” to “necessary, self-existent, pure actuality,” you need additional classical premises:\n\n- **Essence/existence distinction:** In contingent things, essence and existence are distinct. In the ultimate ground, they are identical. Its essence is to exist.\n- **Act/potency:** The ultimate ground cannot have unrealised potency, because potency requires an actualiser. So it is pure actuality.\n- **Simplicity:** Pure actuality cannot be composed of parts, because composition implies dependence on those parts.\n- **Immateriality:** Matter involves potency and composition. So pure actuality is immaterial.\n- **Immutability:** Pure actuality cannot change, because change requires potency.\n- **Timelessness:** If it is immutable and the ground of time, it is not temporal in the ordinary sense.\n- **Uniqueness:** This requires a separate argument: two unrestricted pure actualities cannot differ, because difference requires limitation or lack.\n\nSo the classical conclusion is:\n\n> If the core argument is granted, and if the classical essence/existence and act/potency frameworks are also granted, then there exists a unique, simple, immaterial, immutable, timeless, self-existent, necessary ground—the prime mover—on which all contingent reality depends.\n\nThis is a **conditional proof**. It is valid if the premises are accepted. It is not an unconditional proof that forces assent from someone who rejects the PSR, rejects classical act/potency, or accepts brute fact or infinite regress.\n\n---\n\n## What the core argument does not prove\n\nIt does **not** prove by itself:\n\n- that the ground is conscious,\n- that it has a will,\n- that it is omnipotent,\n- that it is omniscient,\n- that it is omnibenevolent,\n- that it created the universe *ex nihilo*,\n- that it is the God of any particular religion.\n\nThose require further arguments. They are traditional extensions, not immediate consequences of the contingency argument alone.\n\n---\n\n## On physicalism and mathematics\n\n**Physicalism:**  \nThe accurate claim is not “physicalism is not self-existent” — physicalism is a doctrine, not an entity. The accurate claim is:\n\n> Fundamental physical reality cannot be the ultimate self-existent ground unless it can be shown that physical nature entails existence. Physics alone does not show this. But that is an epistemic limitation, not a metaphysical proof that physical reality is contingent.\n\n**Mathematics:**  \nMathematical truth gives abstract necessity, not concrete causal efficacy. On a Platonist view, mathematical objects exist abstractly, but they are causally inert. They cannot be the first cause. This does not by itself identify the ultimate ground.\n\n---\n\n## On brute fact and infinite regress\n\nBrute fact and infinite regress are **logically possible**. They are not formal contradictions. But they are not stable ultimate explanations if you demand a complete explanation.\n\n- **Brute fact:** says something just exists with no reason in its nature. It is uncaused but not self-explanatory. It leaves ultimate reality unintelligible at the most fundamental level.\n- **Infinite regress:** explains each member by another, but never explains the series as a whole. It defers explanation forever.\n\nSo the classical ground is not the only logically possible stopping point. It is the most rationally satisfactory stopping point **if** you accept the demand for complete explanation.\n\n---\n\n## The most rigorous conclusion\n\n> If at least one contingent concrete being exists, if every such being has a sufficient ontological ground, and if no series composed entirely of derivative grounds can constitute a complete ground, then at least one non-derivative ground of contingent reality exists.  \n>   \n> If the classical essence/existence and act/potency frameworks are also accepted, this ground can be argued to be necessary, self-existent, simple, immaterial, immutable, and timeless.  \n>   \n> Uniqueness requires a separate individuation argument.  \n>   \n> Identifying this ground with the omniscient, omnipotent, perfectly good Creator God of classical theism requires still further premises.\n\nThat is the strongest version. It is a serious, coherent, conditional proof of a prime mover. It is not an unconditional proof of the full classical theistic God. Each model parameter is mapped to a measurable neural quantity, and the four subject conditions (S1–S4) become operational tests that can be applied to existing and new datasets.\n\n---\n\n## Level 2 Research Protocol: Operationalizing the Decombination Model\n\n### 1. Parameter-to-Neural Observable Map\n\nThe first requirement is a principled correspondence from the model parameters \\((J, g, a, \\beta, \\theta, \\phi)\\) to measurable neural quantities. The table below proposes the mapping, grounded in existing neuroscience literature.\n\n| Model Parameter | Neural Correlate | Measurement | Rationale |\n|---|---|---|---|\n| **\\(J\\)** (coupling strength) | Effective connectivity | Granger causality, DCM, or transfer entropy from fMRI/EEG | \\(J\\) controls spatial coherence; higher \\(J\\) means stronger inter-regional coupling[reference:0] |\n| **\\(g\\)** (stabilization) | Neural gain / excitability | Slope of evoked response, E/I balance proxies | \\(g\\) stabilizes amplitude; analogous to gain control |\n| **\\(a\\)** (vacuum amplitude) | Baseline oscillatory power | Alpha/beta power at rest | Sets the \"default\" amplitude of neural order parameter |\n| **\\(\\beta\\)** (inverse temperature) | Arousal / noise level | Lempel-Ziv complexity (LZc), spectral entropy | Higher \\(\\beta\\) = lower noise; psychedelics increase LZc[reference:1] |\n| **\\(\\theta\\)** (integration threshold) | \\(\\Phi_{\\max}\\) or \\(\\mu[\\Phi_{\\max}]\\) | IIT 3.0 metric from fMRI[reference:2] | Direct measure of integrated information |\n| **\\(\\phi\\)** (self-model quality) | Predictive coding error / self-referential BOLD | DMN activity during self-referential tasks | DMN is implicated in self-modeling |\n\nThis mapping is not arbitrary. Psychedelics increase LZc (lower effective \\(\\beta\\)) and reduce network modularity (lower effective \\(J\\))[reference:3]. Anesthesia suppresses fronto-parietal feedback (lower \\(J\\)) and reduces \\(\\Phi_{\\max}\\)[reference:4]. Split-brain severing reduces interhemispheric \\(J\\) to near zero[reference:5]. DID involves state-dependent changes in frontal-parietal activation[reference:6].\n\n---\n\n### 2. Experimental Paradigms and Data Requirements\n\nFour experimental domains can test the model. Each exploits a natural perturbation of one or more parameters.\n\n#### 2.1 Psychedelics (Psilocybin, DMT, LSD)\n\n**Model prediction:** Psychedelics reduce effective \\(J\\) and increase effective \\(\\beta^{-1}\\) (noise), driving the system below the coherence threshold. This should reduce the number of coherent domains (alters) while increasing entropy.\n\n**Data already available:**\n- Simultaneous EEG-fMRI under DMT (N=20)[reference:7]\n- EEG under psilocybin (LZc, alpha power)[reference:8]\n- fMRI functional connectivity under psilocybin (network modularity)\n\n**Analyses:**\n- Estimate effective \\(J\\) from fMRI functional connectivity using the inverse of the covariance matrix (precision matrix). Specifically, \\(J_{\\text{eff}} \\propto -\\log(|\\Lambda_{ij}|)\\) where \\(\\Lambda\\) is the precision matrix.\n- Estimate effective \\(\\beta^{-1}\\) from EEG LZc: \\(\\beta^{-1}_{\\text{eff}} \\propto \\text{LZc}\\).\n- Apply spectral clustering to the graph Laplacian of the functional connectivity matrix. Count the number of clusters \\(K\\) at each time point.\n- Compute S1 (integration) for each candidate cluster using conditional mutual information[reference:9].\n- Compute S2 (dissociation) via the Markov blanket criterion: \\(I(\\Psi_A; \\Psi_R \\mid \\Psi_B) \\le \\varepsilon\\)[reference:10].\n\n**Predictions:**\n- Under placebo: \\(K \\ge 2\\), with each cluster satisfying S1–S2.\n- Under psychedelic: \\(K\\) decreases (domains merge), S1 fails for larger clusters (integration drops below \\(\\theta\\)), and LZc increases.\n- The critical point where \\(K\\) changes should correspond to a bifurcation in \\(J_{\\text{eff}}\\).\n\n#### 2.2 Anesthesia (Propofol, Sevoflurane)\n\n**Model prediction:** Anesthesia increases effective \\(\\beta\\) (reduces noise) and decreases effective \\(J\\) (reduces coupling), driving the system toward the homogeneous state \\(\\Psi = 0\\).\n\n**Data already available:**\n- Resting-state fMRI under propofol at multiple sedation levels[reference:11]\n- Simultaneous EEG-fMRI under sevoflurane[reference:12]\n\n**Analyses:**\n- Estimate \\(J_{\\text{eff}}\\) from fMRI precision matrix at each sedation level.\n- Estimate \\(\\beta_{\\text{eff}}\\) from EEG spectral entropy.\n- Compute \\(\\mu[\\Phi_{\\max}]\\) (IIT 3.0) for each resting-state network[reference:13].\n- Apply the spectral clustering analysis at each level.\n\n**Predictions:**\n- As sedation deepens, \\(J_{\\text{eff}}\\) decreases, \\(\\beta_{\\text{eff}}\\) increases, and \\(K \\to 1\\) (one homogeneous domain).\n- At loss of consciousness (LOC), S1 fails entirely (integration below threshold).\n- The transition from wakefulness to LOC should show a bifurcation at a critical \\(J_{\\text{eff}}\\).\n\n#### 2.3 Split-Brain (Callosotomy)\n\n**Model prediction:** Severing the corpus callosum reduces interhemispheric \\(J\\) to near zero, producing two independent domains (one per hemisphere).\n\n**Data already available:**\n- Resting-state fMRI in callosotomy patients[reference:14]\n- Behavioral data on interhemispheric transfer\n\n**Analyses:**\n- Compute the graph Laplacian of the functional connectivity matrix for each hemisphere separately.\n- Apply spectral clustering within each hemisphere.\n- Compute S1 (integration) within each hemisphere and S2 (dissociation) between hemispheres via the corpus callosum as Markov blanket.\n\n**Predictions:**\n- Each hemisphere satisfies S1–S2 independently.\n- The interhemispheric Markov blanket (corpus callosum) shows \\(I(\\Psi_L; \\Psi_R \\mid \\Psi_{\\text{CC}}) \\approx 0\\).\n- The number of domains \\(K = 2\\) in complete callosotomy, \\(K = 1\\) in partial callosotomy with spared fibers[reference:15].\n\n#### 2.4 Dissociative Identity Disorder (DID)\n\n**Model prediction:** DID represents a metastable regime where multiple domains (alters) coexist within a single brain, with state-dependent boundaries.\n\n**Data already available:**\n- Task-based fMRI during identity-state switching[reference:16]\n- Behavioral reaction times and self-relevance processing\n\n**Analyses:**\n- Estimate \\(J_{\\text{eff}}\\) and \\(\\beta_{\\text{eff}}\\) for each identity state separately.\n- Apply spectral clustering to the functional connectivity matrix within each state.\n- Compute S1–S2 for each candidate alter during its active state.\n- Compute S3 (self-model) via predictive modeling of boundary states: \\(\\mathcal{E}_{\\text{self}} = I(B_{t+1}; M_t \\mid B_t) - I(B_{t+1}; M_t^{\\text{null}} \\mid
